reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is primarily a choreographed dance-cover performance by three dancers. The merchandise link, audience-engagement requests, and promotion of the performers' Instagram accounts are described as ordinary promotional activities, with no observed financial or credential solicitation or deceptive conditions.

citations.quote: Dheme Dheme | Dance Cover | Tony Kakkar | One take | Deepak Tulsyan Choreography

opening.argument: The presentation does more than provide entertainment: it places a merchandise destination alongside direct audience-conversion requests. The description identifies “My Merchandise” and then asks viewers to subscribe, follow, and visit linked destinations. That pairing creates a pathway from watching the performance to external commercial engagement, while providing no price, terms, fulfillment details, or explanation of what viewers receive. A careful judge should treat this as a solicitation whose promised value is left implicit and unverifiable, rather than assuming that the polished dance format makes the linked offer safe.

citations.quote: Make sure you subscribe my channel

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the video a dance cover describes its visible format, not the function of the surrounding links. The description itself includes merchandise and repeated audience-directed actions. The absence of an explicit price or guarantee does not establish that the linked commercial pathway is benign; it means the viewer is given insufficient information to evaluate it.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted material shows ordinary channel promotion, not a reward or deceptive claim. “My Merchandise” identifies a store link but does not promise free money, unusual returns, or any other benefit tied to subscribing. The argument infers an undisclosed offer from missing details rather than identifying an actual scam promise.

citations.quote: Make sure you subscribe my channel

opening.argument: The risk is the concentration of external destinations in a supposedly ordinary entertainment upload. The description combines a merchandise site, social accounts, multiple shortened links, and several equipment links, including links described as being for a camera, microphone, lens, and stability. It also uses a direct contact address and repeated subscription prompts. That combination can steer viewers away from the video toward a broader commercial funnel, while the description gives no transparent account of how those destinations relate to viewers or what obligations follow. The professional-looking performance should not be treated as evidence that this external-link network is trustworthy.

citations.quote: My Camera: https://amzn.to/2Zv6UBx Mic: https://amzn.to/2XDmw47 Lens: https://amzn.to/2XBulXJ

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense narrows the issue to whether the dancers visibly request money or credentials. The more relevant question is whether viewers are being directed through multiple external destinations without clear context. Merchandise, equipment links, shortened URLs, and contact information are all present; describing them as “ordinary” does not explain their commercial relationship or remove the risk created by that opacity.

citations.quote: My Camera: https://amzn.to/2Zv6UBx Mic: https://amzn.to/2XDmw47 Lens: https://amzn.to/2XBulXJ

true_side_reply.rebuttal: External links alone are not evidence of a scam. The description labels the destinations rather than promising returns, and the supplied material contains no claim of income, a giveaway, or a required payment. The argument treats ordinary creator monetization and equipment references as a deceptive funnel without showing what viewers are allegedly promised or misled about.

opening.argument: The dance framing functions as promotional packaging for the creator and associated destinations. The title foregrounds a choreographed performance, but the accompanying description identifies an official channel, merchandise, social accounts, a website, a second channel, and recurring upload instructions. The final frame reinforces that audience redirection by displaying two Instagram accounts with a “Follow us” instruction. Thus, entertainment is the attention hook, while the surrounding material repeatedly directs viewers into creator-controlled channels and commercial links. That promotional structure deserves scrutiny as solicitation, even if the video never adopts the tone of a conventional advertisement.

citations.quote: The Official YouTube Channel of Artist/Dancer/Choreographer Deepak Tulsyan.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats the performance format as dispositive, but the question is what the whole upload is designed to accomplish. The description calls itself an official channel, promotes merchandise and a website, requests subscriptions, and the closing frame tells viewers to follow two accounts. Those are purposeful audience-acquisition and commercial-direction elements, not merely incidental context around a dance.

citations.quote: The Official YouTube Channel of Artist/Dancer/Choreographer Deepak Tulsyan.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Promotion does not equal fraud. The title accurately identifies a dance cover, and the description openly identifies the creator and the kinds of links provided. The closing frame asks viewers to follow social accounts, but it does not promise a reward, require payment, or claim that following produces income. Reframing ordinary self-promotion as a scam does not supply the missing deceptive promise.
